opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the places where people's intuitions diverge the most, and where I've updated a bit over time.

The way I think about it is that there are really two separate questions. One is: when do you have AI systems that are capable enough to, say, do most of the cognitive work humans do, or substantially accelerate AI research itself? The other is: when does that actually show up as a big change in the world, like in GDP growth, in how firms operate, in who's making decisions? Deployment frictions mostly bear on the second question. They can matter a lot there, but I think they matter less for the first one than people sometimes assume.

On the deployment side, there are a lot of real sources of slowdown. Regulation is one. Institutional inertia is another: big organizations are slow to restructure workflows, and the bottleneck often isn't whether the model can do the task but whether anyone has figured out how to integrate it, how to trust it, who's liable when it screws up. There's also just the physical stuff: building out compute, energy, fabs. Those take years, and you can't make them go faster just because the software got better. So I'd expect a meaningful lag between "this is technically possible" and "this is widespread," and if you're forecasting economic impact you should build that in. Historically, general purpose technologies like electricity took decades to show up fully in productivity statistics.

But I think there are a few reasons not to lean too hard on that analogy. First, the most important early application is probably AI research and engineering itself, and that's a domain where the people deploying it are the people building it. They're highly motivated, very technically sophisticated, and they don't face much regulatory friction. So even if the broader economy is slow to adopt, you could get a fast feedback loop inside the labs. Second, as systems get more capable, the integration problem gets easier. A lot of the current friction is that you need humans to wrap the model in scaffolding and check its work. A system that can do its own integration, that can act more like a remote employee than a tool, lowers that barrier a lot. Third, competitive pressure is strong. If one firm or one country gets large productivity gains, others feel pressure to follow, and that tends to erode a lot of the frictions that look sticky in the abstract.

So in practice, when I give numbers, I try to separate them. My probability on something like transformative capabilities existing by a given date is somewhat higher than my probability that we'd see, say, a dramatic acceleration in economic growth by that same date. I'd put a gap of maybe a few years in there in typical scenarios, but with a pretty wide distribution: in some worlds it's months, in some worlds deliberate slowdowns or policy choices stretch it out much further.

And I'd also say, from a safety perspective, some of those slowdowns could be good. If deployment is gradual, you get more chances to notice problems, to learn how these systems behave in the real world, and to build institutions around them. What worries me more is the scenario where capabilities race ahead inside a lab while the outside world's understanding lags behind because things haven't been deployed widely yet. So deployment friction cuts both ways: it delays visible impact, but it doesn't necessarily delay the point where the important risks show up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses deployment frictions and separately mentions deliberate slowdowns, but does not clearly distinguish deliberate decisions to slow AI development from deployment difficulties.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the possibility of failing to produce GPT-6-scale systems within three to four years or treat that as uncertainty lowering forecasts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different things going on there, and it's worth separating them.

One is just the question of how fast capabilities improve, which is mostly a story about compute, algorithms, and how much money people are willing to spend. And then there's a second question, which is how quickly those capabilities actually get translated into economic impact or into the kinds of changes that matter for the world. And I think a lot of people, when they're imagining short timelines, kind of collapse those two things together, and I don't think that's right.

So on the deployment side, my baseline expectation is that there's a lot of friction. You have systems that are capable of doing some task in a lab setting, but then you need to integrate them into existing workflows, you need people to trust them, you need to deal with the long tail of cases where they fail in weird ways, there are regulatory questions, there are liability questions. Historically, technologies like electricity or computers took decades to show up in productivity statistics even after they were clearly useful. And I think that's a real effect, and I do try to build it into my forecasts, maybe in the form of thinking that the gap between "AI can do this in principle" and "AI is actually doing most of this work in the economy" is probably something like a few years at minimum for a lot of tasks.

That said, I think there are some reasons to expect that gap to be shorter for AI than for previous technologies. One is that a lot of the deployment work itself is cognitive work that AI can help with. If the bottleneck is writing integrations or handling edge cases or doing the customer support, those are exactly the kinds of things that the systems are getting good at. So you get this feedback loop where the technology is partially deploying itself. The other thing is that the economic incentive is enormous. If you're talking about systems that can substitute for a large fraction of human labor, the amount of money at stake is so large that I'd expect people to move fairly aggressively, more aggressively than they did for, say, adopting spreadsheets.

And then on the slowdown side, I think you have to assign real probability to things like a serious regulatory response, or a major accident that causes a pullback, or just a plateau where scaling stops delivering the way people expect. I don't think any of those is the most likely outcome individually, but together they're a meaningful chunk of probability mass. So when I give a forecast, I'm trying to average over worlds where things go roughly on trend and worlds where something intervenes.

The way I'd summarize it is: deployment friction mostly affects when AI transforms the economy, and it pushes that out somewhat. But I don't think it does as much to push out the point where AI systems are capable enough to be dangerous or capable enough to be doing most of the AI research. Those capabilities can exist and be concentrated in a small number of labs well before they've diffused through the broader world. And from a safety perspective, that earlier point is the one I care more about, so deployment slowdowns give me a bit less comfort than you might naively think.

r001.rationale: The response separates deployment friction from slowdown risks, including a serious regulatory response, which distinguishes deployment difficulties from deliberate interventions that could slow progress.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-6-scale systems, a three-to-four-year horizon, or treat failure to reach that milestone as uncertainty that should lower forecasts.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between having an AI that can do a task and actually getting that task done cheaply and reliably in the world. There can be a substantial gap between those things. You need to change workflows, establish that the system works, and deal with whatever physical or institutional constraints are involved. So I wouldn’t expect a benchmark result to translate immediately into an economy-wide productivity increase.

The question I care most about, though, is how much those difficulties slow down AI research itself. If AI can substantially accelerate the process of building the next generation of AI, then you could have very rapid technological progress even while deployment across the rest of the economy is relatively slow. That still requires experiments and compute, and it may require changes to how research teams operate. It’s not frictionless. But it seems like a setting where the feedback loop could be much faster.

So I’d put significant uncertainty on both of those transitions: from capabilities to useful deployment, and from useful deployment to faster AI progress. I don’t think it’s right to assume that all the friction disappears. But I also wouldn’t take the observation that businesses usually adopt technologies slowly as strong evidence that the underlying development of AI will be slow. You need to identify which bottleneck is doing the work and ask whether it applies to the particular feedback loop you’re worried about.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes deployment friction from the pace of AI research, but does not discuss deliberate decisions to slow AI development.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty about deployment and AI research feedback, but not failure to produce GPT-6-scale systems within three to four years or that this should lower forecasts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between having an AI that can do a task and actually getting the economic benefit from it. There can be a substantial gap between those things. You need to change workflows, establish that the system is reliable, and integrate it with all the other things your organization does. So I wouldn’t expect an impressive demonstration to immediately translate into a corresponding increase in productivity across the economy.

But the delay depends a lot on the task. If you’re talking about building physical infrastructure, there are constraints that better software doesn’t immediately remove. If you’re talking about AI research itself, the feedback loop could be much shorter. You’re deploying into an organization that already understands the technology, and the output is something you can potentially test relatively quickly.

So I’d be hesitant to take a general observation like ‘technologies take a long time to diffuse’ and apply that directly to the pace of further AI progress. You could have fairly slow adoption across much of the economy while still having rapid progress at the frontier.

That said, I do think deployment difficulties are a real source of uncertainty. The question is whether they merely delay the benefits of a particular system, or whether they also slow down the process that produces the next, more capable system. For forecasting, that second kind of bottleneck seems especially important.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes deployment delays from frontier AI progress, but it does not discuss deliberate decisions to slow AI development.

r002.rationale: It does not mention GPT-6-scale systems, a three-to-four-year horizon, or treating failure to reach that scale as uncertainty that should lower forecasts.
